stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.det.ch.justification: Q1: yes. The elaborated signatures quantify over `{R : Type u} [CommRing R]`, `{n : ℕ}`, `A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) R`, and `x : R`. The apparent `CommRing` hypothesis is not added drift: the source context states, “For the rest of Section ... we fix a commutative ring K.” The first declaration asserts exactly `(A + x • 1).det = ∑ P, ...det * x ^ (n - #P)`, matching “det(A + x I_n) = sum_{P subseteq [n]} det(sub_P^P A) · x^{n-|P|}.” Here `P : Finset (Fin n)` ranges over every subset of `[n]`; `Matrix.submatrix` is documented as having entries `M (r i) (c j)`, and `P.orderEmbOfFin` is the increasing bijection onto `P`, so its determinant is precisely the principal minor indexed by P. The second declaration sums over `k ∈ Finset.range (n + 1)` and filters all P by `P.card = n - k`, exactly representing `k=0,...,n` and `|P|=n-k`. Scalar multiplication `x • (1 : Matrix ...)` is the pointwise matrix scalar action on the identity, hence `x I_n`. Q2: yes. The informal displayed chain gives each of the two formal equalities separately after the standard encodings `K ↦ R`, `[n] ↦ Fin n`, and subsets `P ↦ Finset (Fin n)`. Conversely, the two Lean declarations share the same left-hand side, so together they give the full informal equality chain. There are no extra mathematical hypotheses, restricted ranges, or altered definitions.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.det.x-.justification: The source context fixes the coefficient type exactly as required: “For the rest of Section ... we fix a commutative ring K.” The elaborated Lean signature likewise quantifies over `{R : Type*} [CommRing R]`, with `{n : ℕ}`, `x : R`, and `d : Fin n → R`. The referenced definition is `constPlusDiagMatrix x d := fun i j => x + if i = j then d i else 0`, which is exactly the informal matrix having diagonal entries `x+d_i` and off-diagonal entries `x`. The conclusion `(constPlusDiagMatrix x d).det = (∏ i : Fin n, d i) + x * ∑ i : Fin n, ∏ j ∈ Finset.univ.erase i, d j` exactly represents “det F = d_1...d_n + x sum_i d_1...hat(d_i)...d_n”: `Fin n` indexes the n entries, and `univ.erase i` omits precisely the i-th factor. Thus Q1 is yes: every Lean instance supplies the informal identity over the fixed commutative ring. Q2 is also yes: the informal data translate directly to `d : Fin n → R` and the defined matrix, yielding exactly the Lean equality. There are no additional hypotheses or restricted index ranges.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.sf.pier.justification: Q1: yes. Q2: yes. The elaborated signatures quantify over `{N : ℕ} {R : Type} [CommRing R]` and state `hsymm (Fin N) R n * schur mu = ∑ lam ∈ horizontalNStripPartitions mu n, schur lam` and, respectively, `esymm (Fin N) R n * schur mu = ∑ lam ∈ verticalNStripPartitions mu n, schur lam`. These hidden binders match the source's standing convention, quoted as “Fix a commutative ring K. Fix an N ∈ ℕ” and its polynomial ring `K[x₁,…,x_N]`; `Fin N` is merely the zero-based indexing equivalent of the source's `[N]`. Mathlib defines `hsymm` as “the sum over all the degree n monomials” and `esymm` as “the sum over all the degree n squarefree monomials,” matching `h_n` and `e_n`. The project definition `schur lam := ∑ T ∈ ssytFinset lam, T.toMonomial` matches the source definition `s_λ := ∑_{T∈SSYT(λ)} x_T`; its tableaux have entries in `Fin N`, are row-weak, and column-strict, exactly as the source requires. Finally, the formal summation domains match “λ/μ is a horizontal [or vertical] n-strip”: `horizontalNStripPartitions` and `verticalNStripPartitions` require containment, respectively `μ_i ≥ λ_{i+1}` or `λ_i ≤ μ_i + 1`, and size equation `|λ| = |μ| + n`. The horizontal enumerator's explicit finite upper bounds do not narrow the intended domain: the bounds for later rows follow from the horizontal-strip condition, while the first-row bound follows from containment and the size equation. Thus both formal declarations express precisely the two informal Pieri identities.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.sf.schu.justification: Q1: yes. The elaborated signature universally quantifies `{N : ℕ} {R : Type} [CommRing R]` and concludes `(schur (R := R) ⟨lam, hlam⟩).IsSymmetric`; specializing to `R = ℤ` and positive `N` yields the informal claim. The partition binder also matches the source notion: `lam : Fin N → ℕ` with `hlam : ∀ i j, i ≤ j → lam j ≤ lam i` is precisely a weakly decreasing N-tuple. Moreover, Mathlib documents `MvPolynomial.IsSymmetric` as invariance under permutations of variables, matching “is a symmetric polynomial.” Q2: no as stated. The source context says, “We work over a fixed positive integer N and the polynomial ring P = ℤ[x_1, x_2, ..., x_N],” whereas the declaration's folded section binders quantify over every natural `N`, including zero, and every coefficient type `R` satisfying `[CommRing R]`. Its referenced definition likewise has the genuinely coefficient-parametric body `noncomputable def schur ... : MvPolynomial (Fin N) R := ∑ T ∈ ssytFinset lam, T.toMonomial`. Thus the informal integer-coefficient, positive-dimensional assertion does not itself assert the declaration's additional cases over arbitrary commutative rings and `N = 0`. The difference enters at `SymmetricFunctions.schur_isSymmetric_jacobiTrudi` through the implicit binders `{N : ℕ}`, `{R : Type}`, and `[CommRing R]`, together with the `R` parameter in `SymmetricFunctions.schur`. To match the recorded source exactly, specialize the conclusion to `R := ℤ` and restrict `N` to the source's positive setting, for example with `[NeZero N]`; alternatively, revise the informal statement and its Schur-polynomial definition to explicitly quantify over arbitrary commutative coefficient rings and allow `N = 0`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-cor.lgv.bin.justification: Q1: yes. The elaborated signature is `∀ {k : ℕ} (a b : Fin k → ℕ), (∀ i j : Fin k, i ≤ j → a j ≤ a i) → (∀ i j : Fin k, i ≤ j → b j ≤ b i) → 0 ≤ (Matrix.of fun i j => ↑((a i).choose (b j))).det`. Thus `a` and `b` are precisely length-`k` sequences of nonnegative integers, and the hypotheses encode exactly the informal chains `a₁ ≥ a₂ ≥ ⋯ ≥ aₖ` and `b₁ ≥ b₂ ≥ ⋯ ≥ bₖ` after the standard shift from `Fin k` indices `0,…,k-1` to indices `1,…,k`. The conclusion is the determinant over `ℤ` of the matrix whose `(i,j)` entry is `(a i).choose (b j)`, cast from `ℕ`, and asserts it is nonnegative. The library docstring confirms that `Nat.choose n r` is “the number of `r`-element subsets in an `n`-element set. Also known as binomial coefficients,” while `Matrix.of` merely “Cast[s] a function into a matrix.” Hence the formal conclusion implies the displayed informal inequality. Q2: yes. Given any informal `k`, sequences, and the two decreasing chains, representing the sequences as functions `Fin k → ℕ` supplies exactly `ha` and `hb`, and the informal determinant is exactly the formal `Matrix.det`. There are no hidden section binders or additional hypotheses in the elaborated declaration. The `k = 0` case is also consistent with Lean’s standard meaning of `ℕ` and the empty determinant convention.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-cor.lgv.cat.justification: Q1: yes. The elaborated signature is `LGV.catalan_hankel_det (k : ℕ) : (catalanHankelMatrix k).det = 1`, with no hidden hypotheses or restricted range. The referenced definition is `def catalanHankelMatrix (k : ℕ) : Matrix (Fin k) (Fin k) ℤ := Matrix.of fun i j => (catalan ((i : ℕ) + (j : ℕ)) : ℤ)`. Thus its zero-based entry `(i,j)` is `catalan (i+j)`. Under the reindexing `i = I-1`, `j = J-1`, this is exactly the informal entry `c_{I+J-2}` for `1 ≤ I,J ≤ k`. Mathlib's recursively defined `catalan` denotes the source's sequence because `catalan_eq_centralBinom_div` states `catalan n = n.centralBinom / (n + 1)`, while `Nat.centralBinom_eq_two_mul_choose` states `n.centralBinom = (2 * n).choose n`; together these give the quoted informal definition `c_n = 1/(n+1) binom(2n,n)`. The coercion of these natural-number entries to `ℤ` is the standard determinant coefficient ring and does not alter the claimed equality. Q2: yes. The informal statement quantifies over the same `k ∈ ℕ` and says the determinant of precisely this finite matrix is `1`, which directly gives the Lean equality after zero-based reindexing and integer coercion. The informal equality between the indexed notation and the displayed matrix is only an expansion of the same matrix, not an additional independent assertion. The `k = 0` case is also compatible: `Fin 0` gives the empty matrix, whose determinant is `1`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.fps.su.justification: Q1: yes. The elaborated hypothesis `hf_mulable : ∀ (n : ℕ), ∃ M, ∀ (J : Finset I), M ⊆ J → coeff n (∏ i ∈ J, f i) = coeff n (∏ i ∈ M, f i)` is exactly the unfolded project definition of a multipliable family: `Multipliable a := ∀ n : ℕ, CoeffFinitelyDeterminedInProd a n`, where `CoeffFinitelyDeterminedInProd a n := ∃ M : Finset I, DeterminesCoeffInProd a M n` and `DeterminesCoeffInProd a M n := ∀ J : Finset I, M ⊆ J → ...`. Its conclusion is the same predicate applied to `fun i => (f i).subst g`. Mathlib defines `subst a f` as substitution of `a` into `f`, and its coefficient formula uses `coeff d f` multiplied by coefficients of `a ^ d`; thus `(f i).subst g` is `f_i ∘ g`, in the same order as the informal fragment `(f_i \circ g)`. Finally, the formal hypothesis `hg : constantCoeff g = 0` is precisely the informal `[x^0]g = 0`. Therefore the Lean statement implies the informal statement. Q2: yes. Unfolding informal multipliability gives exactly the formal hypothesis and desired conclusion, so the informal statement implies the Lean statement. The elaborated ambient binders `{K : Type} [CommRing K]` supply the coefficient-ring setting, while `[DecidableEq I]` only supports `Finset I` operations and is an encoding requirement rather than an additional mathematical restriction (classical decidable equality is available for an arbitrary index type).

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.det.det.justification: Q1: yes. The elaborated signature is `∀ {R : Type u} [CommRing R] {n : ℕ} (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) R) (d : Fin n → R), (A + Matrix.diagonal d).det = ∑ P, (A.submatrix (P.orderEmbOfFin ...) (P.orderEmbOfFin ...)).det * ∏ i ∈ Pᶜ, d i`. This matches the informal formula `det (A+D) = ∑_{P⊆[n]} det (sub_P^P A) · ∏_{i∈[n]\P} d_i`: finsets of `Fin n` represent all subsets of `[n]`, `Pᶜ` is the complement in the full finite index set, and `P.orderEmbOfFin` enumerates P in increasing order, exactly as the source definition of `sub` requires. Mathlib documents `Matrix.diagonal d` as having entry `d i` on the diagonal and zero when the indices differ, matching the source's explicit `D = (d_i [i=j])`. The implicit `[CommRing R]` is not drift: the governing source convention says, `For the rest of Section ... we fix a commutative ring K`, while the Lean declaration generalizes uniformly over that fixed arbitrary ring. Q2: yes. Given the informal diagonal matrix D and its diagonal entries, the source explicitly says `so that D = (d_i [i=j])`; hence D is exactly `Matrix.diagonal d`, and the Lean equality is the informal equality after the standard identification of the source's one-based `[n]` with `Fin n`. Conversely, every `Matrix.diagonal d` is a diagonal D with those entries, so the Lean parameterization does not narrow the informal quantification. The final sentence calling these determinants 'principal minors' is explanatory terminology rather than an additional propositional claim; the project also defines `principalMinor` using this same principal submatrix determinant.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.sf.jt-e.justification: Q1: No. Q2: Yes, only as a restricted specialization. The informal theorem chooses the determinant size independently: “Let M ∈ ℕ be such that both λᵗ and μᵗ have length ≤ M,” while the surrounding source fixes an independent number N of polynomial variables. The source explicitly clarifies for Jacobi–Trudi that tableau entries remain in “[N]” when the partitions are M-tuples. In contrast, the elaborated signature has a single parameter N: `lam mu lamt muT : Fin N → ℕ`, forms an `N × N` determinant, and uses `esymm (Fin N) R`. Thus N simultaneously controls the row representation of λ and μ, the padded transposes, the determinant size, and the polynomial alphabet. The module itself confirms this discrepancy: “In the source, M is the length of the partition tuples … while N is the number of variables … We use a single parameter N for simplicity.” Moreover, because `NPartition.IsTranspose lam lamt` is two-sided and both functions have domain `Fin N`, it restricts the represented partitions and their transposes to fit inside an N-by-N box, whereas the informal theorem only requires a freely chosen M large enough for the transposes. There is a second restriction at the target binder `hcontained : ∀ i, mu i ≤ lam i`: the informal statement quantifies over “two partitions” without this hypothesis, and its referenced skew-Schur definition assigns no tableaux, hence polynomial zero, when μ is not contained in λ. The formal `SkewPartition` instead has a mandatory `contained` field, so `skewSchur` cannot even express those source cases. Consequently, the general informal theorem specializes to the formal equality, but the formal theorem cannot imply the independent-M or noncontained cases. Making the source meaning statable requires changing the dependency definitions `SkewPartition`, `SkewSSYT`, and `skewSchur` so the shape dimension and tableau alphabet dimension are separate and noncontained shapes yield zero; then `jacobiTrudi_e` must introduce an independent binder `M`, take `lamt muT : Fin M → ℕ`, and use a `Matrix (Fin M) (Fin M)` while retaining `esymm (Fin N) R`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.sf.jt-h.justification: Q1: Yes. The elaborated declaration quantifies over `{N : ℕ}`, `{R : Type u}`, `[CommRing R]`, `lam : Fin N → ℕ`, and `hlam : ∀ i j : Fin N, i ≤ j → lam j ≤ lam i`, so `⟨lam, hlam⟩` is exactly an N-partition. Its conclusion is `schur (R := R) ⟨lam, hlam⟩ = (jacobiTrudiMatrixH (R := R) lam (fun _ => 0)).det`. The referenced definition expands the matrix entry to `hsymmExt ((lam i : ℤ) - (0 : ℤ) - (i.val : ℤ) + (j.val : ℤ))`, while `hsymmExt` is `if 0 ≤ n then hsymm (Fin N) R n.toNat else 0`. Thus the right side is precisely the determinant of `(h_{λ_i-i+j})` with the usual negative-index convention. Although Lean uses zero-based `Fin N` indices, replacing source indices i,j by `i.val + 1,j.val + 1` leaves `-i+j` unchanged. The matrix has row and column type `Fin N`, matching the informal range `1 ≤ i,j ≤ N`. The left side uses `schur`, defined as `∑ T ∈ ssytFinset lam, T.toMonomial`, matching the source definition of `s_λ` as the sum of tableau monomials. Q2: Yes. The informal phrase "For non-skew Schur polynomials (μ = 0)" and formula `s_λ = det((h_{λ_i-i+j})_{1 ≤ i,j ≤ N})` implicitly require λ to be an N-partition; `hlam` merely packages that requirement and is not an added restriction. The ambient source convention fixes an arbitrary commutative ring and N, matching Lean's implicit `{R}` with `[CommRing R]` and `{N}`. The target explicitly uses N for both the determinant size and the N-variable Schur polynomial, as Lean does through `Fin N`; unlike the more general source theorem with an independent partition length M, no independent M appears in this informal target. Therefore each statement implies the other.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.sf.lr-z.justification:
Q1: No. Q2: No. There are two decisive differences. First, the source fixes only "a commutative ring K" and defines the ambient ring as "P ... K[x_1,...,x_N]", whereas the elaborated target has the additional binder `[IsDomain R]` in `theorem littlewoodRichardson [IsDomain R]`. This restricts the theorem to integral-domain coefficient rings, so the Lean theorem does not cover the source's arbitrary commutative ring. The restriction enters through the target binder and ultimately through the dependency `AlgebraicCombinatorics.alternant_rho_isRegular`, whose formal signature also assumes `[IsDomain R]`; it should instead establish the required regularity over the chapter's arbitrary commutative ring, or the target should be proved by another argument allowing removal of `[IsDomain R]`.

Second, the source definition says: "If we don't have μ⊆λ, then we agree that there are no Young tableaux of shape λ/μ." The Lean definition instead unconditionally sets `skewYoungDiagram lam mu := {c | mu c.1 < c.2 ∧ c.2 ≤ lam c.1}` and `Tableau lam mu := {c // c ∈ skewYoungDiagram lam mu} → Fin N`. Thus, when `mu` is not contained in `lam`, Lean can retain boxes from rows where `mu i < lam i` and consequently admit tableaux, while the source admits none. The same mismatch propagates into `skewSchurPoly`, whose body unconditionally sums over Lean's semistandard tableaux. Since the target quantifies over every three N-partitions without a containment hypothesis, these malformed-shape cases are included. To make the formalization faithful, `Tableau`/`skewYoungDiagram` and `skewSchurPoly` should implement the source convention by yielding no tableaux, and hence the zero skew Schur polynomial, whenever `¬∀ i, mu i ≤ lam i`; merely adding a containment hypothesis to the target would omit source cases rather than formalize them. For contained shapes, the remaining equation and the definitions of semistandardness, content, and `IsYamanouchi` match the quoted informal rule.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.sf.skew.justification: Q1: no. Q2: yes. The informal statement quantifies over “any partitions λ ⊇ μ” and asserts that “s_{λ/μ} is a symmetric polynomial.” In the intended finite-variable setting, the partition length and the number of polynomial variables are independent. The module itself confirms this: “In the source, M is the length of the partition tuples (for Jacobi-Trudi), while N is the number of variables,” followed by “We use a single parameter N for simplicity in this formalization.” The elaborated declaration instead has one implicit binder `{N : ℕ}` and takes `lam mu : Fin N → ℕ`, while its conclusion concerns `MvPolynomial (Fin N) R`. This forces the partitions to have exactly the same indexing dimension as the variable set. Consequently, for a fixed number N of variables, skew shapes represented using M-partitions with M > N cannot even be supplied to the theorem. Thus the Lean theorem proves only the dimension-diagonal cases M = N and does not imply the unrestricted informal claim; the informal claim does imply those cases. The mismatch enters through the definitions: `SkewPartition (N)` contains `NPartition N`, `SkewSSYT (s : SkewPartition N)` has entries in `Fin N`, and `skewSchur` returns `MvPolynomial (Fin N) R`, all using the same parameter. The intended independent-dimension theorem cannot be stated with this `skewSchur`, so the verdict is unstatable rather than ordinary drift. To make it faithful, generalize the tableau and polynomial definitions to separate parameters M and N, for example `SkewSSYT (s : SkewPartition M)` with entries in `Fin N` and `skewSchur : SkewPartition M → MvPolynomial (Fin N) R`, then state the theorem with `lam mu : Fin M → ℕ` and independent `{M N : ℕ}`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-cor.lgv.kpa.justification: Q1: Yes. The elaborated signature quantifies over exactly the informal setting: `{K : Type} [CommRing K]`, `{k : ℕ}`, `w : ArcWeight integerLattice K`, and `A B : kVertex (ℤ × ℤ) k`. Its hypotheses `hxA : xDecreasing A`, `hyA : yIncreasing A`, `hxB : xDecreasing B`, and `hyB : yIncreasing B` exactly encode the four displayed weak orderings. In particular, `xDecreasing A` unfolds to `∀ i j : Fin k, i ≤ j → xCoord (A j) ≤ xCoord (A i)`, while `yIncreasing A` unfolds to `∀ i j : Fin k, i ≤ j → yCoord (A i) ≤ yCoord (A j)`, with `xCoord := Prod.fst` and `yCoord := Prod.snd`; the same applies to B. The lattice also has the intended meaning: `integerLattice.arc u v := (v.1 = u.1 + 1 ∧ v.2 = u.2) ∨ (v.1 = u.1 ∧ v.2 = u.2 + 1)`, namely east and north unit steps. The formal conclusion `(pathWeightMatrix integerLattice_pathFinite w A B).det = nipatWeightSum integerLattice_pathFinite w A B (Equiv.refl (Fin k))` expands on the left to the matrix with entries `∑ p ∈ pathsFromTo ... (A i) (B j), pathWeight w p`, and on the right to the sum over nonintersecting path tuples from A to B of `pathTupleWeight`, matching the informal equation. The informal preliminary claim, quoted as “there are no nipats from A to σ(B) when σ ∈ S_k is not the identity,” is represented by the declared dependency `LGV.no_nipats_nonidentity`, whose conclusion is `nipatSet ... A (permuteKVertex σ B) = ∅` under the same sorting hypotheses and `hσ : σ ≠ Equiv.refl (Fin k)`. Thus it is not lost merely because the target declaration records the resulting simplified equality. Q2: Yes. The informal assumptions supply precisely the formal binders and hypotheses, and its displayed determinant identity is precisely the formal conclusion after unfolding `pathWeightMatrix`, `nipatWeightSum`, `pathWeight`, and `pathTupleWeight`. No additional mathematical restriction is introduced by the formal signature; the hidden `CommRing K` binder is explicitly present in the referenced weighted LGV setting (“Let K be a commutative ring”).

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-cor.pars.pn.justification: Q1: Yes. The elaborated theorem quantifies exactly over positive naturals, `∀ n > 0`, matching “For each positive integer n”. Its `partitionCount` reduces to `Nat.Partition.partitionCount`, whose body is `fun n => Fintype.card n.Partition`; `Nat.Partition` is defined as multisets of positive integers whose sum is `n`, so this is the intended partition number `p(n)`. Its `pentagonalNumber` body is `((3 * k - 1) * k / 2).toNat`, and the project proves `(pentagonalNumber k : ℤ) = (3 * k - 1) * k / 2`, matching `w_k`. The formal summand sign, `if k.natAbs % 2 = 1 then 1 else -1`, equals `(-1)^(k-1)` for every nonzero integer `k`: it is positive for odd `|k|` and negative for even `|k|`, producing the displayed `+,+,-,-,+,+,-,-,…` pattern at `w_1=1, w_{-1}=2, w_2=5, w_{-2}=7, …`. The formal range `{k : ℤ // k ≠ 0 ∧ pentagonalNumber k ≤ n}` is the finite-support form of the informal `k∈ℤ; k≠0`: terms with `w_k>n` have negative `n-w_k` and are conventionally zero, while the formal statement omits them and uses natural subtraction only where `w_k≤n`. Thus the formal equality entails both the compact recurrence and its displayed expansion. Q2: Yes. Conversely, the informal recurrence, restricted to its nonzero terms `w_k≤n`, is exactly the formal `tsum`; the subtype is finite because pentagonal numbers grow, so `∑'` introduces no convergence strengthening. The cast of the natural-valued partition count into `ℤ` merely supplies the additive group needed for alternating signs. No additional mathematical hypothesis or restriction appears.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.fps.inf.justification: Q1: yes. The elaborated hypothesis `hM_approx : ∀ k ≤ n, ∀ J : Finset I, M ⊆ J → coeff k (∏ i ∈ J, f i) = coeff k (∏ i ∈ M, f i)` exactly expresses the informal condition “for all k ≤ n and J ⊇ M, [x^k](∏_{i ∈ J} f_i) = [x^k](∏_{i ∈ M} f_i).” The project definition `DeterminesCoeffInProd` confirms that these `J` are intended to be finite supersets: “for every finite superset J of M,” with body `∀ J : Finset I, M ⊆ J → ...`. The formal premise `hg : constantCoeff g = 0` is precisely `[x^0]g = 0`. Its conclusion `∀ J : Finset I, M ⊆ J → coeff n (∏ i ∈ J, (f i).subst g) = coeff n (∏ i ∈ M, (f i).subst g)` exactly matches the informal conclusion. Mathlib defines `subst (a) (f)` as “Substitution of power series into a power series,” and `(f i).subst g` elaborates as `PowerSeries.subst g (f i)`, hence denotes the stated outer-inner composition `f_i ∘ g`. Q2: yes. Conversely, the informal statement supplies every substantive formal binder and equality. The hidden section binders `{K : Type*} [CommRing K]` provide the ordinary coefficient-ring setting for these products and substitutions, while `[DecidableEq I]` is only an implementation instance required for `Finset` products and does not mathematically narrow the class of index sets. Thus neither direction introduces an additional mathematical hypothesis or changes a quantifier, coefficient, product, or composition orientation.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.jtp.par.justification: Q1: yes. The elaborated signature is exactly “partitionGenFun * pentagonalSeries = 1” in ℤ⟦X⟧, matching the informal “P·Q = 1.” The referenced definitions give “partitionGenFun := PowerSeries.mk fun n => partitionCount n,” with partitionCount an alias for Nat.Partition.partitionCount, so it is precisely the informal “P = ∑_{n≥0} p(n)x^n.” Likewise, “pentagonalSeries := PowerSeries.mk fun n => (pentagonalCoeff n : R),” where pentagonalCoeff is (-1)^k.natAbs when n = pentagonalNumber k and zero otherwise, and “pentagonalNumber (k : ℤ) := ((3 * k - 1) * k / 2).toNat.” Since the pentagonal numbers are nonnegative and injective, this coefficientwise definition is exactly the locally finite formal series “Q = ∑_{k∈ℤ} (-1)^k x^{w_k}”; using k.natAbs does not change the sign because (-1)^k = (-1)^|k|. Thus the Lean equality implies the stated generating-function identity. Q2: yes. Interpreting the informal P and Q as formal power series with integer coefficients gives exactly the two Lean definitions, so the informal identity implies the Lean equality. There are no additional binders, hypotheses, typeclass restrictions, or narrowed index ranges in the elaborated theorem.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.sf.schu.justification: Q1: yes. Q2: yes. The informal claim is exactly "Let λ be an N-partition" and "a_{λ+ρ} = a_ρ · s_λ". The elaborated Lean signature is `{R : Type u} [CommRing R] {N : ℕ} (lam : Fin N → ℕ) (hlam : IsNPartition lam) : alternant (lam + rho N) = alternant (rho N) * schurPoly lam`. Its implicit ring and dimension binders match the source convention "Fix a commutative ring K. Fix an N ∈ ℕ"; they are not added restrictions. `IsNPartition lam` is defined as `∀ i j : Fin N, i ≤ j → lam j ≤ lam i`, exactly a weakly decreasing N-tuple of natural numbers. Addition on `Fin N → ℕ` is pointwise, matching the source's "addition on ℕ^N is defined entrywise", and `rho N` has body `fun i => N - 1 - i.val`, representing `(N-1,N-2,...,0)`. The referenced definitions also agree with the informal notation: `alternant α` is `∑ σ, sign σ • xPow (α ∘ σ)` and `alternant_eq_det` identifies it with the source determinant `det((x_i^{α_j}))` (the formal matrix is its transpose, which has the same determinant); `schurPoly lam` is the sum of `xPow (contentTableau T)` over semistandard tableaux of shape `lam/0`, matching `s_λ := ∑_{T∈SSYT(λ)} x_T`. Thus neither direction introduces or omits a mathematical hypothesis, and both statements assert the same polynomial identity over the same arbitrary commutative-ring setting.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.binom..justification: Q1: yes. The elaborated signature is `binomialIdentity {K} [CommRing K] [Algebra ℚ K] [BinomialRing K] [CharZero K] (n : K) (k : ℕ)` with conclusion `∑ i ∈ range (k / 2 + 1), Ring.choose (n + ↑i - 1) i * Ring.choose n (k - 2 * i) = Ring.choose (n + ↑k - 1) k`. Specializing `K` to `ℂ` gives the informal domain.
